facts.title: Born in a Hydrogen Bomb
facts.text: Fermium was first discovered in the radioactive debris of "Ivy Mike," the first thermonuclear (hydrogen) bomb test, detonated by the United States in November 1952 over Enewetak Atoll in the Pacific. Scientists at Los Alamos, Argonne, and Berkeley found that uranium nuclei in the device had captured many neutrons in an instant, then beta-decayed up to element 100. The find was kept secret for years for Cold War security reasons and not announced until 1955.

facts.title: Named for a Nuclear Pioneer
facts.text: The element honors Enrico Fermi, the Italian-American physicist who built the world's first nuclear reactor, Chicago Pile-1, in 1942. Fermi won the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on induced radioactivity using slow neutrons. He died of cancer in 1954, shortly before the element bearing his name was publicly revealed.

facts.title: The Heaviest You Can Bombard
facts.text: Fermium marks an important frontier: it is the heaviest element that can be made in weighable amounts by bombarding lighter elements with neutrons in a reactor. For elements beyond fermium (mendelevium and up), this neutron-capture route fails because the relevant fermium isotopes fission or decay too quickly. To make heavier elements, scientists must switch to firing whole atomic nuclei at targets in accelerators.

facts.title: A Vanishingly Brief Existence
facts.text: Every isotope of fermium is radioactive, and the most stable one, fermium-257, has a half-life of only about 100.5 days. More commonly studied fermium-255 lasts barely 20 hours. This means fermium can never accumulate; any sample is constantly decaying away into other elements.

facts.title: Nowhere in Nature
facts.text: Fermium does not occur naturally on Earth in any detectable quantity, and none is believed to exist naturally anywhere in the cosmos today. Although it can in principle form during the rapid neutron-capture (r-process) in supernovae and neutron-star mergers, its isotopes decay far too fast to survive the journey of cosmic time. Every fermium atom that has ever been studied was manufactured by humans.

facts.title: Spontaneous Splitting
facts.text: Fermium-256 has a striking decay habit: instead of just emitting an alpha particle, most of its atoms undergo spontaneous fission, literally splitting in two without any outside trigger. Its half-life for this process is only about 2.6 hours. This made fermium isotopes important test cases for physicists studying how and why heavy nuclei tear themselves apart.

facts.title: Studied a Few Atoms at a Time
facts.text: Because so little fermium can ever be made, much of its chemistry has been explored using "tracer" techniques with just a handful of atoms in solution. Researchers infer its behavior by watching how those atoms move through chemical separations rather than by handling a visible lump of metal. In water it normally forms the Fm3+ ion, like its neighboring actinides.

facts.title: An Unusual Two-Plus State
facts.text: Although fermium usually behaves with a +3 charge, chemists have shown it can be coaxed into a +2 oxidation state more easily than the actinides just before it. This reflects the growing stability of a filled 5f electron shell as you move across the actinide series. Such subtle electronic trends help scientists test theories about chemical periodicity at the very edge of the periodic table.

facts.title: A Discovery Naming Dispute
facts.text: The right to name elements 99 and 100 became entangled in Cold War politics and scientific rivalry. American teams led by Albert Ghiorso and Glenn Seaborg proposed honoring Fermi and Einstein, but the secrecy around the bomb test complicated the credit and timing of the announcement. The names einsteinium and fermium were eventually accepted internationally.

facts.title: No Job Outside the Lab
facts.text: Fermium has no commercial, industrial, or medical applications, and it plays no role in any living organism. Its extreme scarcity, high cost of production, and rapid radioactive decay make it useful only for fundamental scientific research. Studying it helps chemists and physicists understand the limits of nuclear stability and the behavior of the heaviest elements.
